Herd immunity, also known as community immunity, is a concept that describes the protection of a population from infectious diseases when a large percentage of individuals are immune to a particular pathogen. Herd immunity is achieved when enough people in a community are vaccinated against a disease that it becomes difficult for the disease to spread from person to person. This protects not only those who are vaccinated, but also those who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons or who have not yet developed immunity through vaccination.

The level of herd immunity needed to protect a community varies depending on the specific disease and the characteristics of the pathogen. For some diseases, a high level of vaccination coverage is necessary to achieve herd immunity, while for others a lower level may be sufficient. Herd immunity can also be achieved through natural exposure to a disease, but this can be risky and may result in more severe illnesses or even deaths.
